title: V. A Sudden Catastrophe
paragraphs: I should mention that Ivan had in fact been summoned before Alyosha. But the court usher had told the President that the witness couldn’t appear just then. He had been taken ill, or had some kind of fit, but he would give his evidence as soon as he was better. Nobody seemed to have heard this, and it only came out later.

For the first moment hardly anyone noticed him come in. The main witnesses, above all the two rival ladies, had already been questioned. For the time being curiosity was satisfied, and the public was almost worn out. Several more witnesses were still to be heard, and after all that had been said they probably had little to add. The time was passing. Ivan walked up with extraordinary slowness. He looked at no one, and he kept his head bowed, as if he were sunk in gloomy thought. His clothes were impeccable, but his face made a painful impression, on me at least. It looked earthy, like the face of a dying man. His eyes were dull. He lifted them and slowly looked around the court. Alyosha jumped up from his seat and moaned, “Ah!” I remember that, but hardly anyone noticed.

The President started by informing him that he was a witness not under oath. He could answer or refuse to answer, he said, but of course he must testify according to his conscience, and so on and so on. Ivan listened and stared back at him blankly. Little by little, though, his face relaxed into a smile. The President looked at him in astonishment, and the moment he finished, Ivan burst out laughing.
“Well, and what else?” he asked in a loud voice.
The court went quiet. Everyone felt that something strange was going on. The President began to look uneasy.
“You ... are perhaps still unwell?” he began, looking around for the usher.
“Don’t trouble yourself, your excellency, I’m well enough, and I can tell you something interesting,” Ivan answered with sudden calm and politeness.
“Do you have some special statement to make?” the President went on, still distrustful.
Ivan looked down and waited a few seconds. Then he raised his head and answered, almost stammering:
“No ... I don’t. I have nothing in particular.”

They began to question him. He seemed to answer unwillingly, in the fewest possible words, and with a disgust that grew more and more plain, though what he said was perfectly rational. To many questions he replied that he didn’t know. He knew nothing about his father’s money dealings with Dmitri. “I wasn’t interested in the subject,” he added. He had heard the prisoner threaten to murder his father. About the money in the envelope, he had heard from Smerdyakov.
“The same thing over and over again,” he interrupted suddenly, looking weary. “I have nothing in particular to tell the court.”
“I see that you are unwell, and I understand how you feel,” the President began.
He turned to the prosecutor and the defense counsel, to invite them to question the witness if they needed to. At that moment Ivan suddenly asked, in an exhausted voice:
“Let me go, your excellency, I feel very ill.”

And with those words, without waiting for permission, he turned and started to walk out of the court. After four steps, though, he stopped, as if he had made a decision. He smiled slowly and came back.

“I’m like that peasant girl, your excellency ... you know the story. How does it go? ‘I’ll stand up if I feel like it, and if I don’t, I won’t.’ They were trying to get her into her sarafan, to take her to church for her wedding, and she said, ‘I’ll stand up if I feel like it, and if I don’t, I won’t.’... It’s in some book about the peasantry.”
“What do you mean by that?” the President asked sternly.

“Why, this.” Ivan suddenly pulled out a roll of notes. “Here’s the money ... the notes that were in that envelope” (he nodded toward the table where the material evidence lay), “the money our father was murdered for. Where shall I put it? Mr. Superintendent, take it.”
The court usher took the whole roll and handed it to the President.
“How can this money have come into your hands, if it is the same money?” the President asked in wonder.

“I got it from Smerdyakov, from the murderer, yesterday.... I was with him just before he hanged himself. It was he who killed our father, not my brother. He murdered him, and I put him up to it ... Who doesn’t want his father dead?”
“Are you in your right mind?” broke involuntarily from the President.

“I should think I am in my right mind ... in the same nasty mind as all of you ... as all these ... ugly faces.” He turned suddenly to the audience. “My father has been murdered, and they act horrified,” he snarled, with furious contempt. “They keep up the pretense for each other. Liars! Every one of them wants his father dead. One reptile devours another.... If there hadn’t been a murder, they’d have been angry and gone home in a bad mood. It’s a spectacle they want! _Panem et circenses_. Though I’m one to talk! Have you got any water? Give me a drink, for Christ’s sake!” He suddenly clutched his head.

The usher went to him at once. Alyosha jumped up and cried, “He is ill. Don’t believe him: he has brain fever.” Katerina Ivanovna rose impulsively from her seat and stared at Ivan, rigid with horror. Mitya stood up and watched his brother hungrily, listening to him with a wild, strange smile.
“Don’t disturb yourselves. I’m not mad, I’m only a murderer,” Ivan began again. “You can’t expect eloquence from a murderer,” he added suddenly, for some reason, and gave a queer laugh.

The prosecutor leaned toward the President, plainly dismayed. The two other judges whispered to each other in agitation. Fetyukovitch pricked up his ears and listened closely. The whole hall was hushed, waiting. The President seemed suddenly to pull himself together.

“Witness, your words are incomprehensible and out of place here. Calm yourself, if you can, and tell your story ... if you really have something to tell. How can you back up your statement ... unless you are in fact delirious?”

“That’s just it, I have no proof. That cur Smerdyakov isn’t going to send you proofs from the other world ... in an envelope. All you people think about is envelopes—one is enough. I’ve got no witnesses ... except one, perhaps,” he said, smiling thoughtfully.
“Who is your witness?”

“He has a tail, your excellency, and that would be irregular! _Le diable n’existe point!_ Don’t pay any attention to him: he’s a paltry, pitiful devil,” he added suddenly. He stopped laughing and spoke almost confidentially. “He’s here somewhere, no doubt—under that table with the material evidence on it, perhaps. Where else would he sit? You see, listen to me. I told him I won’t keep quiet, and he started in about the geological cataclysm ... idiocy! Come on, let the monster out ... he’s been singing a hymn. That’s because his heart is light! It’s like a drunk in the street bawling about how ‘Vanka went to Petersburg,’ and I would give a quadrillion quadrillions for two seconds of joy. You don’t know me! Oh, how stupid all this business is! Come, take me instead of him! I didn’t come here for nothing.... Why, why is everything so stupid?...”
And he began slowly, as if lost in thought, looking around him again. But by now the whole court was in an uproar. Alyosha rushed toward him, but the usher had already taken Ivan by the arm.

“What are you doing?” he cried, staring into the man’s face. Then he grabbed him by the shoulders and threw him violently to the floor. But the police were right there, and they seized him. He screamed in fury. And all the way as they carried him out, he kept yelling and screaming something incoherent.

The whole court was thrown into confusion. I don’t remember everything in the order it happened. I was excited myself and couldn’t follow it all. I only know that later, when things had calmed down and everyone understood what had happened, the usher was reprimanded. He explained, quite reasonably, that the witness had seemed perfectly well. The doctor had seen him an hour before, when he had a slight attack of giddiness, and until he came into the court he had talked quite coherently, so nothing could have been foreseen. In fact, the usher said, Ivan had insisted on giving evidence. But before anyone had fully recovered from this scene, another followed it. Katerina Ivanovna had an attack of hysterics. She sobbed and shrieked loudly, but she would not leave the court. She struggled and begged them not to take her away. Suddenly she cried out to the President:

“I have more evidence to give, and I must give it now ... now! Here is a document, a letter ... take it, read it quickly, quickly! It’s a letter from that monster ... that man there, there!” She pointed at Mitya. “He is the one who killed his father, you’ll see that right away. He wrote to me that he would kill his father! But the other one is ill, he is ill, he is delirious!” she kept crying, beside herself.

The court usher took the document she was holding out to the President. She dropped into her chair and hid her face in her hands. Then she began to sob, convulsively and without a sound, shaking all over and stifling every noise for fear of being thrown out of the court. The document she had handed up was the letter Mitya had written at the “Metropolis” tavern, the one Ivan had called a “mathematical proof.” Alas! Its mathematical force was recognized. Without that letter Mitya might have escaped his doom, or at least the doom would have been less terrible. It was, I repeat, hard to take in every detail. What followed is still confused in my mind. The President must, I suppose, have passed the document straight to the judges, the jury, and the lawyers on both sides. I only remember that they then began examining the witness. The President gently asked whether she had recovered enough, and Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed impetuously:

“I’m ready, I’m ready! I’m quite able to answer you,” she added, evidently still afraid that something would somehow keep her from giving evidence. She was asked to explain in detail what this letter was and how she had come to receive it.

“I got it the day before the crime was committed, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—that is, two days before he committed the crime. Look, it’s written on some kind of bill!” she cried breathlessly. “He hated me at that time, because he had behaved contemptibly and was running after that creature ... and because he owed me that three thousand.... Oh! That three thousand humiliated him, because of his own meanness! This is how it came about, that three thousand. I beg you, I implore you, listen to me. Three weeks before he murdered his father, he came to me one morning. I knew he needed money, and I knew what he wanted it for. Yes, yes—to win that creature and carry her off. I knew then that he had been false to me and meant to abandon me. And it was I, I, who gave him that money. I offered it to him on the pretext that he should send it to my sister in Moscow. And as I handed it over, I looked him in the face and said he could send it whenever he liked, ‘in a month’s time would do.’ How, how could he fail to understand that I was practically telling him to his face, ‘You want money to be false to me with your creature, so here is the money. I’m giving it to you myself. Take it, if you have so little honor as to take it!’ I wanted to prove what he was, and what happened? He took it, he took it, and squandered it with that creature in one night.... But he knew, he knew that I knew all about it. I assure you he understood, too, that I gave him that money to test him, to see whether he had lost every scrap of honor and would take it from me. I looked into his eyes and he looked into mine, and he understood it all, and he took it—he carried off my money!”

“That’s true, Katya,” Mitya roared suddenly. “I looked into your eyes and I knew you were dishonoring me, and I took your money anyway. Despise me as a scoundrel, all of you, despise me! I’ve earned it!”
“Prisoner,” cried the President, “one more word and I will have you removed.”

“That money tormented him,” Katya went on, in a rush. “He wanted to pay it back. He did want to, that’s true. But he needed money for that creature, too. So he murdered his father, and he never paid me back. He went off with her to that village where he was arrested. There he squandered the money he had stolen after killing his father. And the day before the murder he wrote me this letter. He was drunk when he wrote it. I saw that at once, at the time. He wrote it out of spite, and he was certain, absolutely certain, that I would never show it to anyone, even if he did kill him. Otherwise he wouldn’t have written it. He knew I wouldn’t want revenge and ruin him! But read it, read it carefully, more carefully, please, and you will see that he described everything in his letter, all in advance: how he would kill his father and where the money was kept. Look, please, don’t overlook this. There’s one phrase: ‘I shall kill him as soon as Ivan has gone away.’ So he thought out beforehand how he would kill him,” Katerina Ivanovna pointed out to the court, with venomous, spiteful triumph. Oh, it was clear she had studied every line of that letter and caught every meaning hidden under it. “If he hadn’t been drunk, he wouldn’t have written to me. But look, everything is written there in advance, exactly as he committed the murder afterwards. A complete program of it!” she exclaimed frantically.

She no longer cared about any consequences to herself, though no doubt she had foreseen them even a month ago. Even then, perhaps, shaking with anger, she had weighed whether to show the letter at the trial or not. Now she had taken the fatal plunge. I remember that the letter was read aloud by the clerk, right afterwards, I believe. It made an overwhelming impression. They asked Mitya whether he admitted writing it.

“It’s mine, mine!” cried Mitya. “I’d never have written it sober!... We’ve hated each other for plenty of reasons, Katya, but I swear, I swear, I loved you even while I hated you. And you didn’t love me!”

He sank back onto his seat, wringing his hands in despair. The prosecutor and the counsel for the defense began cross-examining her. Mostly they wanted to find out what had led her to hide such a document, and to give her evidence in such a different tone and spirit only a short while before.

“Yes, yes. I was lying just now. I lied against my honor and my conscience. But I wanted to save him, because he hates me so, and despises me!” Katya cried madly. “Oh, how horribly he despises me! He always has. Do you know, he has despised me from the very moment I bowed down to him for that money? I saw it.... I felt it right then, but for a long time I refused to believe it. How often I have read it in his eyes: ‘And yet you came of your own accord.’ Oh, he didn’t understand. He had no idea why I ran to him. He can imagine nothing but baseness. He measured me by himself. He thought everyone was like him!” Katya hissed furiously, in a perfect frenzy. “And he only wanted to marry me because I’d come into a fortune. Because of that, because of that! I always suspected it was because of that! Oh, he is a brute! He was always sure that I would tremble with shame in front of him all my life, because I had gone to him that time. He was sure he had the right to despise me forever for it, and so to stand above me. That’s why he wanted to marry me! That’s how it was, that’s all it was! I tried to win him with my love, a love without limits. I even tried to forgive him his unfaithfulness. But he understood nothing, nothing! How could he, really? He is a monster! I only received that letter the next evening. They brought it to me from the tavern. And that very morning, that very morning, I had wanted to forgive him everything, everything, even his treachery!”

The President and the prosecutor, of course, tried to calm her. I can’t help thinking they were ashamed to be taking advantage of her hysteria and listening to such confessions. I remember hearing them say to her, “We understand how hard this is for you; believe us, we can feel for you,” and so on, and so on. And yet they drew the evidence out of the raving, hysterical woman all the same. At last she described how Ivan had been almost driven out of his mind for the past two months, trying to save “the monster and murderer,” his brother. She spoke with that remarkable clearness which so often comes, if only for a moment, in such overwrought states.

“He tortured himself,” she exclaimed. “He was always trying to make his brother’s guilt smaller, and confessing to me that he, too, had never loved his father, and perhaps even wished for his death himself. Oh, he has a tender, too tender, conscience! He tormented himself with his conscience! He told me everything, everything! He came every day and talked to me as his only friend. I have the honor to be his only friend!” she cried suddenly, with a sort of defiance, and her eyes flashed. “He went to see Smerdyakov twice. One day he came to me and said, ‘If it wasn’t my brother but Smerdyakov who committed the murder’ (for the story was going around everywhere that Smerdyakov had done it), ‘perhaps I am guilty too, for Smerdyakov knew I didn’t like my father and perhaps believed I wanted my father dead.’ Then I brought out that letter and showed it to him. He was completely convinced that his brother had done it, and it overwhelmed him. He couldn’t bear the thought that his own brother was a parricide! Only a week ago I saw that it was making him ill. In the last few days he has talked incoherently in my presence. I saw his mind was giving way. He walked about raving. People saw him muttering in the streets. The doctor from Moscow examined him the day before yesterday, at my request, and told me he was on the eve of brain fever. And all on his account, on account of this monster! And last night he learned that Smerdyakov was dead! It was such a shock that it drove him out of his mind... and all because of this monster, all for the sake of saving the monster!”

Oh, of course, an outpouring like this, a confession like this, is possible only once in a lifetime. At the hour of death, say, on the way to the scaffold! But it was in Katya’s nature, and this was such a moment in her life. This was the same impetuous Katya who had once thrown herself on the mercy of a young profligate to save her father. This was the same Katya who, a little while before, in her pride and chastity, had sacrificed herself and her maidenly modesty in front of all these people. She had told of Mitya’s generous conduct, hoping to soften his fate a little. And now she sacrificed herself again, but this time for someone else. Perhaps only now, only at this moment, did she feel and know how dear that other man was to her! She had sacrificed herself out of terror for him. She had suddenly realized that he had ruined himself by confessing that he, not his brother, had committed the murder. She had sacrificed herself to save him, to save his good name, his reputation!

And yet a terrible doubt crossed one’s mind. Was she lying when she described her old relations with Mitya? That was the question. No, she had not meant to slander him when she cried that Mitya despised her for bowing down to him! She believed it herself. She had been firmly convinced, perhaps ever since that bow, that the simple-hearted Mitya, who even then worshipped her, was laughing at her and despising her. She had loved him with a hysterical, “lacerated” love, out of pride alone, wounded pride, and that love was less like love than like revenge. Oh, perhaps that lacerated love might have grown into real love. Perhaps Katya wanted nothing more than that. But Mitya’s unfaithfulness had wounded her to the depths of her heart, and her heart could not forgive him. The moment of revenge had come suddenly. All that had piled up so long and so painfully in the wronged woman’s breast burst out at once, without warning. She betrayed Mitya, but she betrayed herself as well. And as soon as she had given her feelings full expression, the strain was of course over, and shame overwhelmed her. The hysterics started again. She fell to the floor, sobbing and screaming. She was carried out. At that moment Grushenka, with a wail, rushed toward Mitya before anyone had time to stop her.

“Mitya,” she wailed, “that serpent of yours has destroyed you! See, she has shown you what she is!” she shouted to the judges, shaking with rage. At a signal from the President, men seized her and tried to take her out of the courtroom. She would not let them. She fought and struggled to get back to Mitya. Mitya let out a cry and strained toward her. They overpowered him.

Yes, I think the ladies who had come for the spectacle must have been satisfied. The show had certainly been varied. Next, I remember, the Moscow doctor came in. I believe the President had sent the court usher earlier to arrange medical help for Ivan. The doctor informed the court that the sick man had a dangerous attack of brain fever and had to be taken away at once. The prosecutor and the counsel for the defense questioned him. He said the patient had come to see him of his own accord the day before yesterday. He had warned him then that such an attack was coming, but the man had refused to be looked after. “He was certainly not in a normal state of mind. He told me himself that he saw visions while awake, that he met several dead people in the street, and that Satan visited him every evening,” the doctor finished. Having given his evidence, the celebrated doctor left. The letter produced by Katerina Ivanovna was added to the material evidence. After some deliberation, the judges decided to continue the trial and to enter both unexpected pieces of evidence (from Ivan and from Katerina Ivanovna) in the record.

But I will not set down the testimony of the other witnesses. They only repeated and confirmed what had been said already, each in his own characteristic way. I say again, it was all gathered up in the prosecutor’s speech, which I will quote shortly. Everyone was excited, everyone was electrified by the catastrophe we had just seen, and all of them waited with intense impatience for the speeches for the prosecution and the defense. Fetyukovitch was plainly shaken by Katerina Ivanovna’s evidence. The prosecutor, though, was triumphant. When all the evidence had been heard, the court adjourned for almost an hour. I believe it was exactly eight o’clock when the President took his seat again and our prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, began his speech.
